e.t: Beninu is a Hebrew personal name used to identify one individual in Nehemiah 10:13. It does not function as an ordinary descriptive word in the available record, and its precise significance cannot be determined from the name alone. The occurrence preserves it as a name rather than translating it into a common English meaning. Thus, readers should understand Beninu primarily as the person’s identifying name, while the surrounding verse supplies any further contextual role. This name appears once in the Old Testament corpus.

Adalia is a Hebrew personal name, preserved as “Adalia” rather than translated into an ordinary descriptive word. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Esther 9:8, and identifies a person in the biblical record. Because no lexical definition is provided beyond the name itself, its safest meaning is the personal designation “Adalia,” not an inferred character trait or spiritual idea.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to “mire,” the soft, wet ground associated with marshy or bog-like places. It is a noun used for ground that is difficult to stand or move through. The word occurs four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Job and Ezekiel. Its uses include descriptions of marshy ground in Job and a place in Ezekiel that remains distinct from areas made fresh. The surrounding verse determines its precise force in each occurrence.

This Hebrew verb means “flee”: to escape or run away from danger, threat, or an unwanted situation. It describes purposeful movement away from someone or something rather than simply traveling. The word appears 63 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing a recurring biblical expression for flight and escape. Its ordinary sense remains centered on getting away, whether the person flees openly or leaves to avoid being caught. The precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Hebrew word refers to “fringes” or “wreaths.” It functions as a noun, naming a tangible feature or ornament rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice: once rendered “fringes” and once rendered “wreaths.” These two renderings present the word as referring to something arranged or attached in an ornamental form. Its precise role in either verse depends on the surrounding context, but its basic meaning points to a visible decorative feature.

This Hebrew verb describes being "weaned," marking the point when a child is no longer nursing. It can also function in sentences describing a completed stage or resulting condition. The word occurs 37 times in the Old Testament, so its broader force depends on the sentence where it appears. Its use reaches beyond childhood settings, but the central idea remains a completed transition or result expressed by the verb.

This Hebrew word means “this.” It points to a specific thing, person, or matter already being discussed, helping identify it rather than speaking generally. In the Old Testament, it occurs 13 times, all within Ezra, where it consistently serves this identifying purpose. Its exact reference depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic function is to direct attention to something definite and present in the discussion.

e.t: This word is the personal name “Dathan,” identifying a man in Israel’s history. It functions as a proper name rather than a general description or ordinary action word. Dathan appears ten times in the Hebrew Old Testament, chiefly in Numbers 16, with later mentions in Numbers 26, Deuteronomy, and Psalms. The surrounding evidence connects the name especially with speech and with events involving Dathan as an object of spoken commands or actions. Its meaning is therefore best understood as the name of this biblical person, not as a broader vocabulary term.

This Hebrew word means “he” and functions as a pronoun, pointing to a male person already identified or understood in the sentence. It is a very common Old Testament word, occurring 1,889 times, so its exact reference depends on the surrounding wording. It appears throughout the Hebrew Bible, from Genesis through Malachi, serving mainly to identify or refer back to someone being discussed rather than naming that person directly.

Zabud is a Hebrew personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing an ordinary action, quality, or object. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at 1 Kings 4:5, and is rendered “Zabud.” Because this word functions as a name, its meaning for readers is chiefly identification: it distinguishes a particular person in the biblical record. The surrounding verse is needed to explain that person’s role or significance; the name itself does not provide that additional information.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “hyssop,” the name of a plant. It appears as an object used in several Old Testament commands and actions, including instructions recorded in Exodus, Leviticus, and Numbers. The word occurs 10 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing a specific plant reference rather than a broad abstract idea. Its use in Scripture is connected with commanded acts and with imagery involving cleansing and restoration, while the precise force in any verse depends on that passage’s context.

This Hebrew word is an adjective meaning “lively.” It describes a person or condition characterized by the quality of being lively, rather than naming an action, object, or place. In the Hebrew Bible, it occurs once, at Exodus 1:19, so its normal meaning is represented by this single occurrence. The precise force of the adjective in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text, which is not included here.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to “scum,” the unwanted material that rises or remains in a liquid. It is used five times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all within Ezekiel 24:6, 11, and 12. In those passages, the word functions as the object of statements concerning what happens to the scum. Its basic sense is therefore a residue or impurity associated with liquid, especially something that must be dealt with or removed.

This Hebrew word expresses the act of making someone or something “dedicated”—set apart for a specific purpose. It functions as an action word, describing dedication rather than merely naming a dedicated object. In the Old Testament, it occurs five times across four verses, including passages in Deuteronomy, Kings, Chronicles, and Proverbs. Its repeated use in dedication settings supports the central idea of assigning something intentionally to a particular purpose.

This Hebrew verb means “divided”: it describes separating something into distinct portions or groups. It can refer to people being separated, goods being apportioned, or an arrangement being split into parts. The word occurs 15 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing a consistent sense of division or partition rather than merely describing distance. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being divided and how the surrounding sentence presents the separation.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “account,” referring to something that can be examined, sought, or considered. In its three Old Testament occurrences, it functions as the object of actions involving understanding and inquiry, and it appears in speech. The word therefore points to a matter brought into thoughtful consideration rather than describing an action itself. Its exact force in any one verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Hebrew word means “spin.” It describes the action of turning or twisting fibers into thread or yarn. In the Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in Exodus 35, so its use is narrowly concentrated rather than broadly distributed across Scripture. It functions as an action word, focusing on the work being performed. Its precise role in each occurrence depends on the surrounding verse, but the central idea remains the act of spinning material.

This Hebrew word describes being “afraid”—experiencing fear or dread. It functions as an expression of a person’s emotional response when faced with something threatening, overwhelming, or alarming. In the Old Testament, it occurs five times, appearing in Deuteronomy, Job, and Psalms. Its repeated use in these books shows a normal biblical expression for the inner response of alarm, whether directed toward circumstances, danger, or a serious situation. The surrounding verse determines what causes the person to be afraid in each occurrence.

e.t: This Hebrew word is a personal name, identifying an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. It appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Genesis 36, within genealogical material concerning birth and descent. Its role is connected with a person being named in a family line. The available material does not provide a separate definition or translation meaning for the name, so its safest ordinary sense is the individual’s name itself.

This word refers to the Jezerites, a people group named in the Hebrew Old Testament. It functions as a group designation rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The word occurs only once in the Hebrew corpus, in Numbers 26:49, so its use is narrowly focused on identifying this group. The precise significance of the name in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the established meaning is simply “Jezerites.”

This Hebrew word means “mighty,” describing someone or something as possessing great strength or power. It is used of a person, ruler, or other subject whose ability or force is substantial. The word occurs ten times in the Hebrew Old Testament, especially in Job and Isaiah. Its precise emphasis in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central sense remains strength, greatness, or might.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “throne,” referring to the seat associated with a king’s rule and authority. It is used throughout the Old Testament for royal settings, including succession, ruling, and the establishment of a king’s reign. It can also appear in language involving God’s rule and worship, showing that the word identifies more than furniture: it points to the position and authority represented by the throne. The word occurs 135 times in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus.

This Hebrew word means “double.” It is an action word describing something being made or treated as twofold rather than single. Its basic idea concerns doubling or creating a two-part arrangement. In the Old Testament, it occurs five times across four verses, appearing mainly in Exodus and once in Ezekiel. The surrounding wording determines exactly what is doubled, but the central meaning remains the same: something is regarded or arranged as twofold.

In the latter passage, it appears within a genealogy, where such designations help identify a person’s family or regional connection.

e.t: Ithamar is a personal name, referring to a specific man rather than expressing a general idea or action. In the Old Testament, this name is used for one individual whose life and priestly family connections are recorded across several books. The name occurs 21 times in the Hebrew corpus, from Exodus through Ezra, and is consistently rendered “Ithamar.” Its precise significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage, but the word itself functions as a proper name.

This Hebrew verb means “fight.” It describes engaging in combat or warfare, whether between individuals, groups, or opposing forces. In the Old Testament, it occurs 177 times, so it is used broadly for people actively contending against others. Its appearance in passages across Exodus, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, Samuel, Jeremiah, and other books confirms a consistent connection with armed conflict and opposition. The surrounding passage determines who is fighting and what the conflict involves.

This Hebrew verb means “refuse.” It describes a person or people unwilling to do what is requested or commanded. The word presents refusal as an expressed choice or response, rather than merely describing difficulty or inability. It appears four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, three times in Exodus and once in Jeremiah. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

The word occurs seven times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing in passages from Exodus, Numbers, 2 Samuel, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel. Because the available material identifies the term chiefly by its place-name rendering, its precise geographic setting should be determined from the surrounding passage in each occurrence.

It is used when Scripture describes boundaries, locations, travel, or the position of people and territories. The word occurs 74 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing that it regularly serves as a geographical description rather than naming a person or action. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on what location or boundary the surrounding passage is describing.

The exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to an “acquaintance”—someone known to a person, but not necessarily described as a close family member or intimate companion. It occurs twice in the Old Testament, both times in 2 Kings 12:5 and 12:7. In these occurrences, it functions as something connected with a person in statements about finding, taking hold of, or addressing that acquaintance. The precise force in each verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea is a known person or associate.

This Hebrew noun refers to a “prison,” a place where people are held in confinement. It is used seven times in the Old Testament corpus, including passages describing people shut up or taken away, as well as a reference to those involved in making or managing such a place. Its basic sense is therefore a restrictive holding place, and the surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis falls on the place itself or on people associated with it.

Maasai is a personal name represented by this Hebrew word. It does not have an explicit definition or ordinary descriptive gloss in the available lexical information. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 9:12, and English Bible renderings preserve it as “Maasai.” Thus, its function is to identify a person rather than describe an action, quality, or object. The surrounding verse supplies the specific context for that individual.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to “refreshing,” expressing the idea of being refreshed or receiving refreshing. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Isaiah 28:12, so its ordinary meaning is represented by that single occurrence. The word functions within a speech-related passage and is connected with receiving or experiencing refreshing, while the precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding text.

This Hebrew word means “bed.” It names the physical place where a person lies, especially in descriptions of what someone sees or experiences during sleep. It occurs six times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in Daniel, and each recorded rendering is “bed.” The word therefore points to an ordinary sleeping place rather than an action or an abstract idea. Its precise significance in any passage depends on the surrounding verse.

This Hebrew word is a small particle commonly rendered “now” or “pray.” It can draw attention to the present moment, or introduce an earnest request addressed to someone. Its exact force depends on the sentence in which it appears, but it generally adds urgency or appeal rather than naming an object or action by itself. The word occurs 403 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing that both temporal and pleading uses are part of its normal range.

This Hebrew word means “roaring,” describing a powerful, audible sound. It functions as a word for the sound itself rather than naming a person or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Psalm 38:8 and once in Isaiah 5:30. Those occurrences show that its basic sense concerns an intense sound, while the surrounding verse determines what produces it and what the sound signifies.

This Hebrew word refers to scattering—the act of causing something to spread or be dispersed. It appears once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 30:30, and the available rendering expresses this sense as “scattering.” As a noun-like word, it names the dispersing action rather than describing a person or object. Its precise force in Isaiah 30:30 depends on the surrounding verse and passage, since the verse text is not included here.

This Hebrew word means a “thicket,” referring to a tangled mass of bushes or trees. It functions as a noun, naming dense vegetation rather than an action, person, or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 4:7. Because it appears only once and no verse text is provided here, its central lexical sense is clear, while the precise force of the word in that sentence belongs to its surrounding context.

e.t: Amnon is a personal name identifying a man in the Hebrew Old Testament. It is not a descriptive word or action; it functions as a person’s name in the narrative. The name occurs 28 times in 22 verses, concentrated in 2 Samuel and also appearing in 1 Chronicles. Its related passages include birth, speech, commands, and death. Accordingly, when readers encounter Amnon, they should understand it as the individual’s name, while the surrounding verse supplies the particular action or circumstance.

This word refers to a “brier,” a plant associated with rough or unwanted growth. It is a Hebrew noun appearing once in the Old Testament, in Isaiah 55:13. Its role there is as a named plant, set alongside other created things in the verse’s imagery. The word itself identifies the plant rather than expressing an action, quality, or abstract idea.

This Hebrew word describes someone or something as “young” or “little.” It points to smallness or youth rather than maturity or great size. The word appears twice in the Old Testament, both times in Job: once rendered “young” and once “little.” Its precise force depends on what is being described in the sentence, but its central idea is a young or small person or group.

This Hebrew word means “eyes,” referring to the organs used for seeing. It is a noun naming the eyes themselves, whether spoken of as one person’s eyes or as multiple eyes in a vision. In the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, it occurs five times: once in Ezra and four times in Daniel. Its basic meaning remains focused on sight and the eyes as bodily features. The surrounding verse determines what is being seen or described, but the word itself names the eyes.

This Hebrew word functions as a personal name, rendered “Alvan” or “Alian.” It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The word occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, in genealogical passages at Genesis 36:23 and 1 Chronicles 1:40. Because no explicit definition is preserved, its meaning is best understood as the individual’s name, while the surrounding passage identifies the person being listed.

This Hebrew verb means “perish”: to be destroyed, ruined, or brought to an end. It describes people, nations, strength, hopes, or paths that disappear or cease to remain. The word can express destruction caused by judgment or circumstances, and it may also describe something failing or vanishing. It occurs 185 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its basic idea is broad: something is lost, undone, or no longer exists in its former condition. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Hebrew word means “wrong.” It describes something as being morally or legally wrong rather than right. In its one Old Testament occurrence, it functions as a predicate—stating what something is or how it stands. The word appears in Habakkuk 1:4, and its precise force there is understood through the surrounding sentence and passage. Its connection with judgment and law reinforces its role in describing a condition recognized as wrong. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding context.

Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central sense remains fear as a powerful response to danger, authority, or threatening circumstances.

This Hebrew verb means “bake,” describing the act of preparing food by cooking it in an oven or similar heated place. It can also appear in the rendered form “baked,” depending on how the sentence expresses the action. The word occurs 25 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, especially in passages involving bread, cakes, or other prepared food. Its ordinary sense is practical and direct: to cook something by heat until it is ready to eat.

Its recorded use is connected with speech and with other words in that verse, but those connections do not by themselves establish a translation.

This Hebrew word means “locks,” referring to locks of hair. It occurs twice in the Old Testament, in Numbers 6:5 and Ezekiel 44:20. Its use is connected with the head, so it identifies hair allowed to remain or treated in a particular way rather than a general object or action. The surrounding verse determines the specific instruction involving these locks.

Pethuel is a personal name, not a common word describing an action, quality, or object. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Joel 1:1, and is rendered “Pethuel.” Because it identifies a person rather than expressing a general idea, its meaning here is chiefly its use as a name. The surrounding verse supplies the information needed to understand that person’s role, which is not included in this word-level explanation.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “neck,” the part of the body connecting the head with the shoulders. It can refer to a person’s neck or to the necks of several people, and it may appear in expressions involving something placed on, around, or against the neck. The word occurs 41 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing a consistent bodily sense across its uses. Its precise force in any passage depends on the surrounding sentence.

This Hebrew word means “form” or “forms,” referring to the shape or arrangement of something. It appears five times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all within Ezekiel 43:11. The word functions as a description of what something is like in its outward design or configuration. Its repeated use in that single verse shows that the passage gives sustained attention to forms or arrangements, rather than presenting this as a broad term scattered throughout the Old Testament. Its precise significance in Ezekiel 43:11 depends on the surrounding verse text and context.

This Hebrew word means “taken,” describing something that has been taken or occupied. It functions as the predicate in its recorded sentence, stating what is true of the subject. The word appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Isaiah 33:20. Because it occurs only there and no verse text is provided here, its broader range cannot be established from repeated usage. Its basic sense remains the idea of something being “taken.”

This Hebrew word refers to a “founder,” describing a person whose work involves forming or handling metal. It functions as a verb, presenting the action associated with such work rather than merely naming the worker. The word occurs 34 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its precise force can vary with the sentence in which it appears. Its uses connect with paths, testing, and crafted images, showing that the word can serve in both ordinary and figurative settings.

e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to meal, the ground grain used in preparing food. It can describe an ingredient measured, mixed, baked, or offered, so its sense is practical and connected with daily nourishment and offerings. The word occurs 14 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing in accounts involving household provision, worship, hospitality, and the feeding of others. Its role is generally that of an object—the meal itself rather than the action of preparing or eating it.

e.t: Argob is a proper name identifying a particular named entity in the Hebrew Scriptures. It is rendered “Argob” and functions as a name rather than as an ordinary descriptive word. The term appears five times in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, in Deuteronomy, 1 Kings, and 2 Kings. Its exact significance in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic lexical role is to designate Argob by name.

This Hebrew word refers to a bald head, describing an exposed or hairless area on the head. It is used four times in the Old Testament, all within Leviticus 13, where the word belongs to descriptions of visible conditions examined under Israel’s laws concerning skin disease. Its basic meaning remains focused on the head and its lack of hair; the surrounding passage determines the precise significance of the condition being described.

This word means “thoughts,” naming what a person thinks or holds in the mind. It functions as a noun, referring to inward thinking rather than an outward action. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Psalm 139, where the rendering is “thoughts.” The word therefore points to the contents of a person’s thinking, whether considered by God or spoken of in relation to Him. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Hebrew word functions as a predicate expressing “is,” stating that something exists or has a particular identity or condition. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, at Psalm 68:16. Its role is connected with describing a relationship involving God and a mountain. This Hebrew word means “broken,” describing something as being broken. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Hosea 8:6. As a descriptive word, it identifies the condition of the thing being discussed rather than naming an action or person. Its precise force in Hosea 8:6 depends on the surrounding context. The passage itself determines how this description functions in that sentence, while the word retains its basic sense.

This Hebrew word means “like,” expressing comparison or likeness between one thing and another. It functions in a sentence by showing that something resembles, matches, or is compared with something else. It occurs three times in the Old Testament, all in Daniel, across two verses. Its use is limited, so the surrounding wording determines exactly what is being compared in each passage.

This Hebrew word refers to “killing,” naming the act itself rather than describing a person or quality. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at 2 Chronicles 30:17, and its recorded rendering there is “killing.” Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic lexical sense is the act of killing. e.t: “Eshbaal” is a personal name identifying an individual in Israel’s genealogical records. It is not presented here as a general action, quality, or object, but as the name of a person. The word occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, both times in 1 Chronicles. Its recorded uses appear within genealogy material, where it is connected with family descent and birth relationships. The precise significance of the name itself is not stated in these occurrences, so its clear role is to identify this individual in the genealogy.

Shelesh is a Hebrew personal name, rendered “Shelesh.” It functions as a name rather than a general description or action. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears once, in 1 Chronicles 7:35, and the available English renderings preserve it as “Shelesh.” Because this word occurs only in a genealogical reference and no verse text is provided here, its identity as a name is the clearest meaning that can be stated confidently.

This Hebrew noun refers to “roots,” the part of a plant that remains beneath the ground and supports its continuing life. It occurs three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in Daniel 4:15, 4:23, and 4:26. In each occurrence, the word identifies what remains connected to the tree underground, distinguishing its hidden foundation from the visible trunk, branches, or leaves. Its basic meaning is therefore concrete and physical; the surrounding verse determines whether that image carries any further significance.

This Hebrew word expresses the idea of “great,” describing something as considerable or beyond the ordinary in extent or importance. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Hosea 13:5. This word is a personal name, rendered “Toi,” rather than an ordinary descriptive term. It identifies the same named person wherever it occurs in the Hebrew Old Testament. The word appears five times, across four verses, all in 2 Samuel and 1 Chronicles. Its meaning is therefore chiefly identificational: it names someone mentioned in those historical accounts, while the surrounding verse supplies the person’s specific role and actions.

This Hebrew word refers to “lies” or “liars”—that is, false claims or people who speak falsely. It is used six times in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, with both the singular idea of falsehood and the plural reference to false speakers represented in English renderings. The word appears in Job, Isaiah, and Jeremiah, showing its use in statements about deceptive speech or those responsible for it. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Hebrew word describes someone or something that has been “chosen”—selected for a particular place, purpose, or standing. It functions as a descriptive word rather than naming the act of choosing itself. In the Old Testament, it occurs 13 times, including passages about people called chosen and about those belonging to God’s chosen people. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding context, but the central idea is selection or appointment.
